entry.title: Rosamund Pike Starring in Body Horror Film ‘Feed’ for ‘Star Wars: The Acolyte’ Creator Leslye Headland
entry.summary: Rosamund Pike will star in the body horror film 'Feed' for 'Star Wars: The Acolyte' creator Leslye Headland.
entry.content:
Rosamund Pike will star in and produce “Feed,” a body horror film from “Russian Doll” co-creator and “Star Wars: The Acolyte” creator Leslye Headland.

The film follows a desperate mother who discovers an obscure collagen supplement that promises to transform her tween gymnast daughter into an influencer. Fame hits fast, but as her daughter goes viral, she undergoes a terrifying transformation. “Feed” was inspired by a 2022 Finnish horror film, “Hatching.” Daniella Isaacs (“People Who Knew Me”) wrote the script.

Headland made her feature debut in 2012 with an adaptation of her play, “Bachelorette.” In 2015, she wrote and directed “Sleeping With Other People.” Both premiered at the Sundance Film Festival.

Related Stories
Letterboxd Finalizing $330 Million Sale to The New York Times
Why ASMR Invaded the Soundscape of ‘La Bola Negra’

Pike was nominated for an Oscar for “Gone Girl.” Her other credits include “Saltburn,” “An Education,” and the James Bond film, “Die Another Day.” She won an Olivier Award for “Inter Alia,” a role she is reprising this fall on Broadway.

“Long have I wanted to make a film that plays anarchically with our obsession with social media and self-improvement, our desire for fame without notable admirable skill and, let’s put it out there, the monstrosity of modern motherhood,” Pike said in a statement. “‘Feed’ deals with all these things. It tracks a Momfluencer, Erin, bent on her daughter’s domination of the digital space. Erin believes that success here will protect her daughter from the horrors of our fickle world… won’t it? ‘Feed’ examines appetite. The dark appetite of online communities; the appetite of a social media landscape that monetizes youth and beauty; the appetite of a mother for her daughter’s success; and the appetite of a teenage girl, hungry for fame, self-empowerment and dominance in her relationship with her single mother. ‘Feed’ is film that plays in the genre space, and plays into our current fears, as parents, as citizens, of the digital world.”

Headland added: “Daniella’s script is audacious, disturbing and deeply human, and Rosamund is among the boldest actors working today. I couldn’t ask for better partners to take on the darker corners of this story and I feel incredibly lucky to be making this film with two women whose work I admire so much.”

The Veterans is overseeing the international sales rights, with CAA Media Finance tackling the U.S. sales. Talks will kick off next week at the American Film Market.

Pike will produce through her Primitive Streak banner, alongside Shelley Browning for Magnolia Entertainment, Steven Schneider for Spooky Pictures, Ara Keshishian and Petr Jakl for ZQ Entertainment, and Sam Ritzenberg for Agile Films. ZQ Entertainment financed the development of the script.

Pike is repped by CAA, United Agents and Magnolia Entertainment; Headland is repped by CAA and Sugar23; Isaacs is repped by Curtis Brown Group.

entry.title: Letterboxd Finalizing $330 Million Sale to The New York Times
entry.summary: Letterboxd is finalizing a deal to be bought by the New York Times Company in a deal valued at $330 million.
entry.content:
Letterboxd, the social networking platform for cinephiles, will soon have new owners. The website is finalizing a sale to The New York Times Company in a deal valuing the website at $330 million, according to a report from the NYT on Thursday.

An agreement has not yet been reached and could still fall apart, but the companies have entered into exclusive negotiations. The $330 million price tag is more than 20 times Letterboxd’s projected earnings in 2026 of about $15 million, the Times reported.

The New York Times would acquire the controlling stake in Letterboxd from Tiny, a Canadian-based public company, which originally picked up a 60 percent stake in 2023 when the website was valued at just $50 million. Tiny has been exploring a sale since April; a deal has finally emerged after film studios, tech executives, and private equity companies all kicked the tires.

Related Stories
Why ASMR Invaded the Soundscape of ‘La Bola Negra’
Two ‘Ramayana’ Cuts Are in Theaters — but Your Best Bet for the Indian Epic Is Clear

The New York Times prevailed over finalists Sony Pictures Entertainment, which has been on a buying spree with trendy outlets for cinephiles like Alamo Drafthouse Cinemas and Cosm, and A24, which for years has been one of the few companies to rival the cultural cache among young film lovers that Letterboxd commands (it helps that Charli XCX is a fan of both).

IndieWire understands that A24 was also in late-stage talks to acquire Letterboxd, with the studio promising Letterboxd’s founders to maintain its independence and its business model unchanged. The Times reported that it has discussed keeping founders Matthew Buchanan and Karl von Randow in place, with each reporting to a Times executive.

Letterboxd has grown significantly since being acquired by Tiny, now reaching 26 million users (though the company does not disclose how many of them are on paid subscriptions.) Its Four Favorites social media segments have proven reliable viral hits. It has attracted young celebrities who have become semi-active users. It also introduced a Letterboxd Video Store that offers digital rental of under-the-radar films or recent festival releases. But the platform has also promised features like the ability to log TV shows that still haven’t materialized to help it grow further.

It’s easy to see how The New York Times Company can help provide scale, though that comes at the risk of making the platform seem a little less cool and independent in the process to its highly discerning userbase. The Times could integrate Letterboxd into its film and TV reviews or its Watching blog, or plan crossovers between Letterboxd and the enormously popular NYT Game. The Pro or Patron subscription tiers of Letterboxd, which remove ads and provide customization options and viewing statistics, could also be bundled with the Times’ other subscriptions like The Athletic, Cooking, or Games. The Times has a goal of reaching 15 million paid subscribers by the end of 2027 and currently has 13.8 million.

entry.title: Why ASMR Invaded the Soundscape of ‘La Bola Negra’
entry.summary: Supervising sound editors Alejandro López and Anna Harrington tell IndieWire about using sound to toggle between timelines in 'La Bola Negra.'
entry.content:
There are a lot of things that can be done in a month, theoretically — but it takes a special kind of close-knit team to take the sound design of a film from picture lock to a premiere at Cannes in a month. Supervising sound designers Alejandro López and Anna Harrington had exactly that challenge with “La Bola Negra,” not only directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo’s most ambitious film to date, but one of the most epic films to come out of Spain in recent memory.

The pair, who’ve worked on Los Javis projects going back to “Veneno,” had a very condensed span to design multiple timelines and storylines that the directors wanted to each have a slightly different sonic feeling.

Related Stories
Two ‘Ramayana’ Cuts Are in Theaters — but Your Best Bet for the Indian Epic Is Clear
‘Everytime’ Review: Sandra Wollner’s Infinitely Beguiling Portrait of Grief in the Digital Age Is One of the Most Haunting Films of the Decade

For the story of Carlos (Milo Quifes), set in 1932 in Grenada, López and Harrington had license to be a little bit more expressive in the sound design to heighten the emotions of the closeted young man accused of being a homosexual during his attempt to join his father’s members-only casino. This tracks with the fact it is, eventually, revealed to be the lost Federico García Lorca play, “La Bola Negra.”

For the 1937 story of Sebastian (Guitarricadelafuente), however, sound was an important, invisible storytelling partner, guiding its protagonist down the path towards rescuing that lost play by falling in love with Lorca’s (Alberto Cortés) former lover Rafael (Miguel Bernardeau) before he’s shot by fascists in the aftermath of the Battle of Santander during the Spanish Civil War. “The importance there was on the off-screen sound to help tell the story,” López told IndieWire. “To have an oppressive atmosphere beyond the frame.”

The gunshots, shouts, vehicles, movement, and marching that López and Harrington craft offscreen all create a kind of strident tide that threatens to wash Sebastian, Rafael, and/or both of them away at key moments in their story. Harrington did a lot of work with the cast of the 1937 section to precisely sculpt ADR, as much to concoct a sense of tragic, and especially Lorquian, chaos as to maintain key pieces of dialogue.

The contemporary 2017 storyline of Sebastian’s grandson Alberto (Carlos González) rediscovering the play his grandfather saved, meanwhile, was meant to be as irritatingly digital and constantly jittering as Alberto’s anxiety is. “Alberto is always surrounded by noise,” Harrington told IndieWire. “Like, he cannot think straight because he’s surrounded by so much noise all of the time.”

But while each storyline has its own specific texture, the sound design team also crafted moments of breathtaking contrasts. There’s invisible but undeniable power when all that noise falls away, where the harsh and heightened soundscapes resolve into softer and more beautiful sonic worlds.

Key among these is a sequence when Sebastian rushes back to the hospital where he’s based and where Rafael is held prisoner, believing that his unrequited (or so he thinks) love may have already been executed while he’d been given a night off. He rushes into the pale dawn light, relieved to find Rafael beaten, but still alive and asleep in a hospital bed. There’s a hush to the moment that brings relief, but not because it’s wholly silent — it’s because of the way that López and Harrington sculpt the sound.

“That moment has really close sound when Sebastian sort of traces [Rafael’s body] and almost touches him. The idea of the shot was for it to be like ASMR. No music at all. Really close, human sounds — the breathing of them both — [were designed] to make that moment immersive. And then I used a low rumble underneath that creates a really strange sensation. It’s like some kind of telluric sound that comes from the Earth. It’s Lorquian.”

“In Lorca’s universe, there are a lot of references to sound,” López added. “We used a lot of resonances with the wind, the ocean, the sound of the waves in the hospital resonating, the winds from the Sierra Nevada, when the old woman appears in the snow. It’s a leitmotif.”

Sonic leitmotifs, sounds that contain emotional and musical resonances, are important to how “La Bola Negra” moves between timelines, but they’re also how the sound design team added texture to the footage of each of the different timelines. The digital 4K world of Alberto tempted the designers to add sound to absolutely everything in the frame, and make it all as sharp and precise as the image. The 35mm footage, by contrast, could be a little more expressive, the textures a little unbounded by what we see. “It’s like the picture is asking for a certain kind of sound,” Harrington said.

It speaks to the strength of the story of “La Bola Negra,” then, that the sound has its own trajectory alongside the image and the characters. And all in about a month.

“Everybody worked like 200% helping each other. [Composer] Raül Refree was calling us. We were calling [Editor] Alberto Gutiérrez, like, ‘Are you cutting this?’ There was a lot of exchanging ideas and helping each other because we had no time at all,” Harrington said. “Everybody wants to do their best, because we knew from the start we were doing something that touches people.”

“La Bola Negra” is now playing in theaters.

entry.title: Two ‘Ramayana’ Cuts Are in Theaters — but Your Best Bet for the Indian Epic Is Clear
entry.summary: What are the differences between the English and Hindi cuts of the 'Ramayana' movie?
entry.content:
“Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” retells a millennia-old Hindu epic on a splashy scale. The Hindi-language studio film — part one of a planned duology — has been released outside India by Sony Pictures, which hopes to make it a cross-cultural hit by courting audiences who don’t normally spend every weekend watching the latest Bollywood fare. Among the strategies for this rollout have been a lavish Comic-Con panel, as well as an English dub of the movie, which was the version shown to press prior to the review embargo. However, language isn’t the only difference; this version is almost half an hour shorter than the Hindi original and excises some make-or-break material.

Related Stories
‘Everytime’ Review: Sandra Wollner’s Infinitely Beguiling Portrait of Grief in the Digital Age Is One of the Most Haunting Films of the Decade
‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Denver Film Festival Top Prize as More Regional Fests Boost Oscar Hopefuls

The Hindi version did eventually screen for press (about a day before the film’s release), but by then, early reviews quickly noted the awkward method of its transposition. Dubbing into different languages is hardly new, but AI-assisted lip syncing to match the actors’ mouth movements gives the English performances a stilted quality. Granted, the in-house program developed for this purpose (named “Brahma AI” after the Hindu creator-god, who features in one of the movie’s many prologues) seems a tad more ethical than most generative AI. The process involves real human beings recording the English lines — in some cases, the original actors themselves — as well as real mouth performances (creepy as that sounds) captured to map onto the original faces. Essentially, its data sets seem to be entirely internal, so the stealing aspect of the wider AI problem isn’t a concern here. However, the effect is distracting by way of exaggerated lip movements, and the English dialogue itself is clunky and emotionally restricting.

This becomes all too clear when watching the Hindi version for comparison, which I managed to on opening day at New York’s Mecca for Indian movies: the labyrinthine, 25-screen AMC in Times Square. The original cut doesn’t make the movie magically great — it still has the same haphazard approach to building action, and the same uncanny CGI — but it does call into question the methods by which Sony has attempted to localize (and globalize) the film for wider viewership. Most obviously: performances are more emotionally convincing in their original form, and the reverb on the original dialogue is much more befitting of a large-scale epic, while the mixing for the English lines conjures images of a claustrophobic studio booth. However, the more baffling comparison is between the different cuts, and how each one affects the story.

The English cut runs 166 minutes, which is about half an hour shorter than the original. With that much of a lag, you’d expect the discrepancies to be obvious early on, but surprisingly, the two films are mostly identical for about the first two hours. They cover largely the same ground, between the origins of the demon king Ravana (Yash), the condensed upbringing of the heroic prince Rama (Ranbir Kapoor), and his eventual exile to the forest alongside his graceful wife Sita (Sai Pallavi) and his devoted brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey). The differences are largely in how scenes play out, especially montages backed by songs.

The film has few traditional dance numbers, but in sequences where wider details from the poem are squeezed into the running time, the English version snips them here and there, removing only minor subplots at first. For instance, when Rama and Sita meet and talk for the first time, Rama’s three brothers can also be seen flirting with various women around the palace, as the prince mentions only wanting to marry Sita if his siblings can be married on the same day. This is absent in the English version, as are shots of the additional three weddings during Rama and Sita’s ceremony. It’s not the most vital thing to include from a plot standpoint, though it arguably gestures toward the nature of the story at large, as one in which Rama tries to stick to his promises, as fate contorts itself in his favor.

Still, this and some other deletions aren’t necessarily missed for much of the running time, like a few extra action beats in existing scenes, and additional shots of Rama and Sita living in their kingdom, Ayodhya, and getting to know its people, in another musical montage. However, they give the story a bit of breathing room, which is never a bad thing. In any case, the most destructive removal is far more noticeable. It arrives about two hours into the Hindi running time, by way of a single dramatic scene (or a trio of scenes in quick succession, depending on how you count them) that makes for the film’s emotional centerpiece, and practically resolves major issues with the English version’s latter half.

Both films conclude with the giant, humanoid bird king Jatayu trying to rescue Sita from a flying chariot when she’s kidnapped by Ravana, in a scene that, while visually dazzling, feels a tad random as the climax to its own movie (rather than a midpoint or inciting incident; the epic has been split quite inelegantly). This in turn leads to a mournful speech from Rama about rejecting his destiny and writing his own path as he plans to march on Ravana’s kingdom of Lanka. In the English cut, this feels like a distinction without a difference, since Rama’s training by various priests and sages has, in fact, been in anticipation of a conflict with Ravana. However, many of these dangling threads feel more emotionally whole in the Hindi version, thanks to the aforementioned scenes, known traditionally as the Bharat Milap, or the meeting with Bharat, Rama’s brother, who was placed on the throne in his stead.

In a subplot wholly absent from the English cut, a royal procession reaches Rama’s humble hut, where Bharat — who knew nothing of the palace conspiracy to replace Rama as king — informs him of their father’s death. In the English version, it’s never clear when, if ever, Rama learns about this major development (which even comes up in the film’s concluding scene), leaving viewers to intuit that it probably happened off screen. However, this isn’t even the only problem the Bharat Milap solves.

After Rama scatters his father’s ashes, the two brothers have an emotional conversation with Lakshmana by their side. Bharat tries to convince Rama to return to Ayodhya and take the throne, but Rama believes this ascetic path has been laid out for him as part of his fate and sacred duty, so he decides to remain in the forest. All the while, Lakshmana harbors a grudge against Bharat, and is angered by Rama’s decision to remain in exile, though he goes along with it as part of his own duty and moral code.

For one thing, this makes Lakshmana make a whole lot more sense as a character in subsequent scenes, in which he occasionally flies off the handle. Without these vital exchanges informing his state of mind, his volatility seems arbitrary (though sadly, neither version manages to make his comedic quips really land). For another, these missing scenes give Rama an actual character arc, and imbue the film with a vital throughline of how various characters approach the idea of divine destiny.

When Sita is kidnapped, and Rama comforts the dying Jatayu — who, by the way, features briefly in these missing scenes as well, making his climactic arrival less sudden — there’s a sense of direct causality to these events. Rama isn’t just a witness to his wife’s abduction and Jatayu’s slaying, but he feels the guilt of having made the decision to remain alone and vulnerable in the first place. When he talks of rejecting destiny and writing his own story, these cease to be the mere platitudes of the English version. They become a direct callback to his own decision-making, in which he chose to follow the lifelong path laid out before him, out of a sense of divine obligation.

This, in turn, affects another scene (albeit a smaller one) in which Ravana and his siblings bicker over whether to kidnap Sita in the first place. The notion of destiny comes up once more, in the idea that Ravana going down this violent path is something the gods might actually want to entrap him in a battle with Rama. Since the movie is a mere first half, its primary hero and villain never interact, and they don’t even feel thematically bound in the English version. In the original cut, these notions of destiny, as laid out by Rama’s chat with Bharat, set the protagonist and antagonist on an unavoidable collision course.

The decision to cut the running time makes roundabout sense, given that one of the few things most Western viewers know about Hindi movies is their historically enormous lengths. However, when Hollywood films like the “Avatar” sequels and “Avengers: Endgame” (and even Indian hits like the Telugu-language “RRR”) draw crowds with three-plus-hour running times, this phantom barrier clearly isn’t insurmountable. Shaving things down to a still-robust 2 hours and 46 minutes isn’t likely to be the deciding factor for many viewers; people tend to round up or down at that length.

While the result feels akin to a Harvey Weinstein-esque interference, this particular decision was, according to the film’s PR team, always the intent of the team behind “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend.” But whatever the impetus for these competing cuts — both of which are now in theaters — the decision to cleave out such a vital emotional and thematic crux, the meeting between the brothers, is utterly confounding. It’s the story’s heart and soul, and erasing it is downright destructive to how the movie plays. So, if you’re deciding between the two versions, the choice should be pretty clear.

entry.title: ‘Everytime’ Review: Sandra Wollner’s Infinitely Beguiling Portrait of Grief in the Digital Age Is One of the Most Haunting Films of the Decade
entry.summary: Sandra Wollner's unforgettable third feature explores the modern world's changing relationship to death.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 10, 2026 during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. 1-2 Special will release the film in limited theaters Friday, November 6, with a wide release to come in February 2027.]

I don’t believe in an afterlife, but that’s OK because the people I love most are never going to die. Not to me. At least, not in the way they used to before our species began to migrate online, to store our memories in the cloud, and to digitally encode the raw data of our existence onto everything we touch. 

My father was born in 1939, the same year that Iowa State College scientists John Vincent Atanasoff and Clifford Berry built the prototype for the first binary-based computer; in the months after he died 75 years later, I often felt the reflex to reach down and call him from the iPhone that fit inside my pocket. To ask if he’d seen the Rangers game, or to tell him that I’d gotten engaged. I knew that he was gone, of course, but the piece of consumer technology I’d used to connect with him when he was alive had created a separate neural pathway between my brain and his being — a crude one-way network that didn’t begin to break down until much later in my grieving process. 

Related Stories
I Remember ‘Rocky’: My Front Row Seat to the Marketing of a Million-to-One Blockbuster
MUBI Has Cleared the Path for Sandra Hüller to Land Multiple Oscar Nominations This Season

A decade later, those pathways have grown exponentially more complicated and convincing. The emergence of AI has led to a variety of ghoulish attempts at deathlessness and resurrection (from bots that feed on your grandma’s Facebook data to the ChatGPT Theodore Roosevelt who Trump was “honored to be with today” at the former’s Presidential Library), but such products and publicity stunts miss the fact that everyone is already being (temporarily) immortalized on a server farm somewhere, the traces of our existence shed into the digital ether like a Pollock-like splotch of invisible ink.

Charlie Kirk’s face is Twitter’s most ubiquitous meme. My long-deceased college friend you’ve never heard of sends me hacked emails full of links to “old pictures they found of us together.” The cancer-stricken hedgehog I fostered for a few months in 2016 still cycles onto my home screen at random sometimes, and he’s now been buried behind a house in suburban New Jersey for longer than he was ever alive. People have always looked for errant glimmers of the dead in the world around them, but now the past runs parallel to — imprints upon, and circles around — the present to a degree that can severely confuse the relationship between the two. 

Sandra Wollner doesn’t believe in an afterlife either, but she’s certainly attuned to the mysteries of this one. Picking up where the equally spectral likes of “Personal Shopper” and “Aftersun” left up, the Austrian writer/director’s mystical and magnificently beguiling “Everytime” takes a rather ambivalent stance towards what happens when people die these days, or at least — per its curious title — towards how we mourn them from inside the flat circle of a temporal overlap where yesterday and tomorrow are folded into the pockets of an ever-expanding now. 

There are no clear answers to be found in this astonishing third feature, which shares a number of thematic similarities with Wollner’s “The Trouble with Being Born,” but retains one crucial difference (that film, about a man who has an implied sexual relationship with a child-sized android coded with the memories of his missing 10-year-old daughter, unsurprisingly had trouble securing American distribution). Indeed, the grounded portraiture of the movie’s first 70 minutes eventually gives way to a final act so cosmic and surreal that it becomes all but impossible to pinpoint the precise location of Wollner’s characters in space-time; to say for certain whether “Everytime” has glitched into another dimension, or if it has invited another dimension to glitch into our own. Initially timeless in its nuanced and deeply recognizable depiction of loss, and then even more so as it gets devoured by the meta-modern flourishes that have fringed its story from the start, this is perhaps the most forward-thinking film I’ve ever seen about the changing face of grief. 

The premise couldn’t be simpler, though Wollner’s incredible prologue — a careful arrangement of low-event long takes that emphasize how people move through spaces in time — trains our eyes to privilege texture over incident. While there’s little to distinguish single mother Ella (“Everyone Else” star Brigit Minichmayr) and her children from any of the other families strolling through the soft orange haze of a summer afternoon in Berlin, our senses pick up on the uneasy tension between the watchfulness of Gregory Oke’s 35mm camera work and the vivid intensity of the film’s sound design (it’s worth noting that Oke also shot “Aftersun”). The voices are close, but the bodies far away. Teenage Jessie (Carla Hüttermann) turns her head to look at an unseen pop as her family walks home through their local metro station, but we don’t think much of it at the moment. It’s probably nothing. And yet, I suppose it could be anything. 

At the very least, that sharp noise is enough to suggest that the film’s environments may not be as benign as they seem, and a silent but soon unbearable tension starts to mount as the day wears on. As Jessie’s boyfriend Lux (Tristán López) comes over to hang out while her kid sister Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling) annoys the shit out of her by banging on a keyboard; as Ella cooks dinner; as Jessie plays “Minecraft” late into the night on an island bathed in the light of a sinking square sun. 

Later, in the waning hours before Jessie’s family is due to leave for a holiday in Tenerife (where she once vacationed as a toddler), Jessie and Lux will sneak out to a dance club, take a few pills, and watch the next day begin from their perch atop the roof of an apartment building. He will note that he’s recently noticed a strange number of seagulls in Berlin, and then fall asleep. She will stand up to film one of them flying past on her iPhone, and then — in one of the most arresting screen images in recent memory, a vertiginous collision of everything and nothing all at once — she will fall off the edge of the building to her death. The city doesn’t notice. The camera scans the treetops. The euphoric synth-pop of David Schweighart’s score kicks in as we suddenly begin to soar through the skies of Jessie’s “Minecraft” world, eventually plunging down through the dirt and into the unrendered levels of code below.

From there, “Everytime” settles into a crushingly quotidian register. Months have passed, and everyone is doing what they can to move on with their lives. Ella takes work calls while visiting her daughter’s grave, while the stoic young Melli texts life updates and other messages to her dead sister’s phone (she’s big on emojis). But things are not as settled as they seem, and Lux’s return from a semester abroad forces Ella and Melli into a more direct confrontation with Jessie’s memory — with the unresolved feelings she left behind. The girls keep running into Lux (and to his nice new girlfriend) around town, and soon begin spending time with him on purpose. They are bound together not only by their shared grief, but also by the unspoken guilt and blame that Lux and Ella can only hope to expiate through each other. 

While Jessie is seldom mentioned by name, the bizarre mutual reliance between a middle-aged woman and her dead teenage daughter’s former boyfriend makes her the subject of every scene (much to the annoyance of people who would prefer to compartmentalize the pain of her loss). Jessie is the reason why Ella and Melli attend Lux’s birthday party; Jessie is the reason why Lux joins Ella for a tense lunch at her ex-husband’s house, and why he begins sleeping over at her apartment. 

But these domestic frictions are — largely, but not merely — a means to an end so far as Wollner is concerned, as her film leverages them to focus on a series of increasingly abstract phenomena. Jessie is certainly the reason why each of the locations we saw her walk through before her death feels haunted when “Everytime” revisits them, but could she also be the reason why the shadow that falls across her bedroom at night appears to resemble a polygonal cube? Why a seemingly pilotless drone shows up to beckon Ella into a pitch-black parking garage? Why the dead girl’s computer glows with an unnatural brightness whenever the lights turn off? 

Wollner’s characters never ask such questions aloud, but she poses them to all three of her leads in a way that compels them to look for signs in the digital detritus that Jessie left behind. Lux is drawn back to the old pictures and voice notes on his phone, while Mille stares at the WhatsApp chat with her sister as if waiting for a response. These signs complement, but never overwhelm, Wollner’s attention to the analog poetry of the natural world — to the shimmer along the surface of a lake, or the sound of the wind rustling through the trees in the woods where Jessie and Lux got high on her last night.

It’s easy to imagine a version of this film that more explicitly addressed how digital technology is transforming how we mourn the dead, but Wollner would rather plumb the mysteries of the present than speculate about the answers of the future; the portals between worlds have already been ripped open, and will only begin to lose their power as they get labeled and branded. 

Eventually, Ella makes the spontaneous decision to bring Mille and Lux to Tenerife for the trip they never got to take. That’s where things get weird, and the math of the universe starts to contradict itself. It would be a terrible disservice to reveal anything specific about what happens next (and so I won’t), but the extraordinary magic trick that “Everytime” pulls off in its final stretch is rooted less in incident than in execution. 

Its ineffable power belongs to how matter-of-factly Wollner tears apart the fabric of her film’s reality at the same time as she threads it together, and how the look on Minichmayr’s slacken face — her restrained but masterful performance a wonder of tightly bottled pain and lingering disbelief — reconciles those opposite energies with the instinctive naturalness of a mother’s love. It also belongs to the almost unquestioning acceptance that Keiling endows within Melli, the young actor’s posture embodying how this movie teeters on the precipice between a child-like vision of the world (soft and malleable) and the more hardened sense of reality that arrives with adulthood.

Wollner may not trace the character’s arc in the legible terms of a typical coming-of-age story, but Melli experiences a remarkable transformation over the course of the film, her petulant first line (“You always leave your stuff lying around!”) assuming an unforeseeable new context by the time we arrive at her closing narration. 

As a medium born from — and once dependent upon smoothing over — the friction between stillness and movement, stasis and change, cinema has always been uniquely adept at conveying the radical effect that technology can exert on how we perceive time and space in the world around us. The switch from celluloid to computer chips saw the movies transform from an illusory art form to a representative one, at the great and continued risk of forfeiting its original power. Engaging in a thrilling and increasingly contested negotiation between 35mm film stock and crude DV video formats, “Everytime” pulls at that tug-of-war from both ends until the uncertain space at the center grows large enough to sail through, and still enough to hang like a painting in the sky.

I am now a father myself, the parent of two young kids whose faces sometimes remind me of my own dad in the same tactile way that people have been survived by their children since before the invention of the wheel. We keep a framed 4×6 photograph of him with a cigar in his mouth on the Blu-ray shelf in our living room, and I sometimes catch my kids talking about it as if the picture itself were their grandfather, rather than just a capture of his likeness. Ask my six-year-old to draw a self-portrait and he’ll sketch you the image of his Roblox avatar. If I ever were to lose him, I wonder how long it would take my nervous system to process that he was gone. 

Like many 21st century parents, my wife and I take photos and videos of our kids throughout the day without thinking, and — after wrestling them to bed at night in an exasperating forever war of attrition — we invariably scroll through our phones and take stock of their cuteness in peace. Stills, videos, stickers, and more, these two-dimensional images, I sometimes feel with an uncertain pang of dismay, are our real children. The versions of them we commit to memory. The after images we see in our dreams. They are the kids we mourn as our son and daughter eagerly outgrow their current models every time you look away for too long, and the ones we would cling to in the unthinkable event that either of them disappeared from this mortal coil before we did.

And so, Wollner’s staggering new film suggests with a tender but uneasy twinkle in its eye, we’ve gradually steeped ourselves in a world that guarantees they never will. How strange and unnatural is that? Compared to the alternative, I fear it may not feel that strange or unnatural at all. 

Grade: A

“Everytime” is screening at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. 1-2 Special will release it in theaters in the United States.

entry.title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Denver Film Festival Top Prize as More Regional Fests Boost Oscar Hopefuls
entry.summary: See all the winners of the 2026 Denver Film Festival, from 'La Bola Negra' to 'I Play Rocky.'
entry.content:
Regional film festivals matter to a movie’s more cosmic position in the awards season, even if it started somewhere like Venice, Toronto, Telluride, Cannes, or even Sundance. They generate excitement from real-world audiences (and often Oscar voters, as in Middleburg, Virginia), and they also help unspool headlines that keep films top of mind for those who follow the race.

The 49th Denver Film Festival, held in the hip, high-altitude Colorado city every year, just wrapped its annual event — which this year ran October 22 to November 1. Denver Film CEO Kevin Smith, artistic director Matthew Campbell, and their team brought out special guests including Carrie Coon, John Leguizamo, John Cho, D’Arcy Carden, Peter Gamble, Indya Moore, Hans Petter Moland, and more to receive prizes and be feted with special tributes. Several of these, including Coon for “The Liberation” and Leguizamo for “The Odyssey,” are in the awards mix. Overall, Denver showcased 130 films, including many awards season favorites.

Related Stories
‘Wild Horse Nine’ Review: Martin McDonagh’s Prickly but Unconvincing CIA Satire Recasts ‘In Bruges’ as the Stuff of a Classic Western
‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

I served on the documentary jury this year and awarded the Maysles Brothers Award to one of the year’s most revered docs. We chose the nonfiction portrait of adolescence “Whispers in May,” winner of this year’s CPH:DOX and from Chinese filmmaker Dongnan Chen, which is still seeking distribution. Per our statement penned with Vanity Fair’s Chris Murphy and producer Justine Suzanne Jones as fellow jurors, it’s “a vivid and compassionate portrait of female friendship in the twilight of adolescence” and “formally daring and emotionally authentic.” Other films in the category included “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” “Edward Said: Between Worlds,” “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” “Nuisance Bear,” and “SUMO: Spirit Weighs Nothing.”

Los Javis’ “La Bola Negra,” which just won the BFI London Film Festival audience award after winning that same prize at TIFF in September, won the Krzysztof Kieslowski Award for Best Feature Film. The Spanish epic about gay desire and Federico García Lorca is locked in for multiple Oscar nominations at this point, with its awards streak going back to Best Director at Cannes in May.

The Audience Award for narrative feature, just as it did at the Virginia Film Festival in October, went to Peter Farrelly’s Sly Stallone behind-the-scenes biopic “I Play Rocky.” The film, starring charming breakout Anthony Ippolito as the “Rocky” star/screenwriter, was the runner-up to “La Bola Negra” in Toronto’s audience award category. “I Play Rocky” is in select theaters Thursday ahead of a November 20 wide release, and its popularity as an audience favorite is proving hard to best at fests.

See the full list of Denver Film Festival winners below.

entry.title: ‘The Weed Eaters’ Lands Expanded Release from Yellow Veil Pictures: New Zealand Cannibal Movie Sets Winter Rollout
entry.summary: Yellow Veil Pictures will release 'The Weed Eaters' in North America after the Australian horror movie debuted on the Letterboxd Video Store.
entry.content:
Yellow Veil Pictures has boarded North American distribution rights for Callum Devlin‘s “The Weed Eaters,” a New Zealand cannibal horror film that notched a best feature win at SXSW Sydney in 2025. The indie banner is planning a winter release.

The deal for “The Weed Eaters” comes after the independent feature first debuted in the Unreleased Gems section of the Letterboxd Video Store, a video-on-demand streaming platform launched by the film-focused social media platform in 2025.

“Yellow Veil are consistently putting out the richest cinematic meals on offer, so it’s a real honour for ‘The Weed Eaters’ to be a part of their roster,” director Devlin wrote in a statement included in the deal’s announcement. “We always knew there was a global audience for this movie. I mean, this film is pretty gross. But the people that are into it are super into it, and we’re more than happy to make movies for the stoner freaks of the world.”

Related Stories
Inside Letterboxd’s Unlikely Distribution Pipeline: How ‘It Ends’ and Other Gems Found Their Way to a Deal
Letterboxd Sale Talks Are Heating Up

“‘The Weed Eaters’ exemplifies what we have come to expect from New Zealand indie films. It’s filled with heart and humor, but this one’s not afraid to get weird and gross along the way,” reads a statement from Yellow Veil.

Exact details on the release plan for “The Weed Eaters” went undisclosed, though Yellow Veil is primarily a digital distribution company with ventures into limited theatrical play.

“The Weed Eaters” follows four friends that have their holiday getaway upended when they stumble upon a strain of marijuana that makes tokers crave the taste of human flesh. The film comes from Sports Team, Horse Bite, and Causeway Films, the Australian banner that was also behind titles like “The Babadook,” “Leviticus,” and “Bring Her Back.”

Prior to “The Weed Eaters,” several other titles featured on the Unreleased Gems section of the Letterboxd Video Store have gone on to land wider distribution, with one of the best-known examples being Neon’s acquisition of the cerebral horror film “It Ends.”

“We would never presume whether these filmmakers want to have a traditional distribution,” Letterboxd’s head of Video Store content Courtney Mayhew told IndieWire in August. “Even if it’s just five really strong ambassadors for these independent gems who will sing their praises and push for it and tell their friends about it … that’s something that has value.”

.

entry.title: ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Review: Martin McDonagh’s Prickly but Unconvincing CIA Satire Recasts ‘In Bruges’ as the Stuff of a Classic Western
entry.summary: John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell are two CIA agents vacationing on Easter Island in McDonagh's sardonic look at American interventionism.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 3, 2026 during the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Searchlight Pictures will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

Another melancholically splenetic Martin McDonagh jag about a banter-mad pair of murderers who go on a boys trip to purgatory (where they search their souls as they wait for death to find them), the prickly but unconvincing “Wild Horse Nine” strains to translate the post-Guy Ritchie bark of “In Bruges” into the language of a classic American Western. In this case, an American Western set on Easter Island and backdropped by Augusto Pinochet’s rise to power in the fall of 1973. 

Related Stories
‘North of North’ Season 2 Review: Netflix’s Defiantly Nice Arctic Sitcom Is for the Warmhearted F**k-Ups
‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

McDonagh’s decision to recast his same old script against the backdrop of such a real and terrible event grants this new telling a welcome sense of scale, both in terms of its characters’ morality, as well as in regards to their greater place in history. But that decision is a double-edged sword that cuts the film off at the knees. Where “In Bruges” kicked off with the killing of a fictional altar boy, “Wild Horse Nine” is overshadowed by the deaths of thousands upon thousands of very real people, and that reality bleeds into the edges of the frame even when the seriocomic absurdity of McDonagh’s writing demands a world of pure invention.

Does the overlap make “Wild Horse Nine” feel glib? Yes, and thank god for that — if not for glibness the movie would lose the majority of its few solid laughs. The problem is that it also makes “Wild Horse Nine” feel as transparently manufactured as the CIA-backed overthrow of a foreign democracy. I can accept that an inexperienced hitman might have a dark night of the soul after shooting an innocent child during confession. By contrast, I struggle to believe that a veteran CIA agent who openly brags about his involvement in the Kennedy assassination would have a come-to-Jesus moment after orchestrating the demise of Salvador Allende. McDonagh has some good fun wrestling with whether or not we should care about such a mottled change of heart, but the point is gradually rendered moot in a movie whose emotions are less credible than its conspiracies. 

The original Company man, Chris (John Malkovich, more locked in than he’s been on screen since “Burn After Reading”) is a natural hinge for the off-kilter comedy that McDonagh builds around him, in that he can be a joy to watch even when you don’t buy a word he’s saying. More than just an ordinary CIA agent, he’s the living personification of America’s efforts to destabilize foreign governments across the 20th century. He was close with Patrice Lumumba until the day the Congolese leader was executed by a firing squad. He was in Cuba to spur on the exiles who failed to overthrow Fidel Castro in 1961. He was even in Dallas, USA on a Friday afternoon in November 1963, doing things his ornery boss MJ (Steve Buscemi) would much prefer he didn’t tell you about.

He traveled to all of those places, and got all of those people killed, with the blithe imperiousness of a flag waving in the wind. Chris says that he’s killed 68 people over the course of his career, and he offers that information as easily as a rumor — in a way that makes it sound like the number could be half that, or double, and it wouldn’t make a difference.

Recently, fate has blown Chris and his office husband/platonic life partner/exasperated straightman Lee (McDonagh vet Sam Rockwell) down south to Chile, where the two of them have been hard at work orchestrating the September 11th coup against the democratically elected socialist president, knowing full well that it would plunge the country into decades of brutal dictatorship. Chris appears to delight in sowing chaos, and the fact that he gets to wear a cute little Panama hat while he does it only boosts his joie de vivre. 

But Chris is fraying at the seams in ways that we can’t see at first — ways that will only begin to reveal themselves when he and Lee decide to celebrate their imminent success with a sightseeing trip to Easter Island, a short 2,300 miles off the Western coast of Santiago. There are still a couple of months to go before the coup, but the wheels are in motion, and there’s little for these men to do for now besides fly to Rapa Nui, look at the “big heads,” flirt with a couple of beautiful young leftists (the prissier but gentler of whom is played by “Ema” mega-talent Mariana di Girolamo), and mordantly reflect upon their role in the awfulness Pinochet will soon inflict upon his own people. That task is complicated and confused by the fact that Chris seems to be losing his memory, which casts Lee in the role of his peevish but loving caretaker. 

“Wild Horse Nine” is only the second feature that’s ever been shot on the ultra-remote soil of Rapa Nui (Kevin Reynolds’ 1994 epic “Rapa Nui” is credited as the first), and McDonagh rightly exalts in the fact that he’s brought Hollywood to the end of the world. The first half of his movie largely adheres to the fiction that Chris and Lee are just on Easter Island to fuck around, which offers a semi-relaxed opportunity for us to take in the sights. Ben Davis’ sun-bleached cinematography renders the hills and beaches of Rapa Nui with the veneer of a lost idyll, the ancient moai statues assuming an especially sacred charge when contrasted against such profane characters. 

Chris bemusedly laughs the statues off with ethnographic glee, mocking one of the shorter figures as a dwarf (in case the “In Bruges” déjà vu wasn’t already strong enough), but it’s clear that he’s shaken by the fact that some of them almost 750 years old. That they’ve stood there in silent tribute to Polynesia’s ancestors as empires rose and fell on faraway shores, each of them a graveyard of forgotten people just like him. By the same token, it’s similarly clear that he’s trying to get at something in his own mind as he and Lee listen to Judy Collins in their rental car, argue over whether or not any Nazis made it into heaven (among other even more aggressively screen-written subjects), and whisper sweet nothings to the wild horses that run about the island, but the specific nature of that something is hard for him to pin down. 

Malkovich has the time of his life with that search for Chris’ last speck of humanity, which shines up from the bottom of his soul as his mind continues to erode. At once both insidiously relaxed and also choked with Catholic guilt, Malkovich’s performance marries the nonchalance of a cowboy to the paranoia of a bounty target. One minute he’s waxing poetic about dinosaurs, and the next he’s rigging his luggage with explosives (maybe) and checking the “Memento”-like reminder notes he’s slipped into his jacket pocket. 

“Wild Horse Nine” loves Chris too much to pretend like we’re not supposed to, but Malkovich never asks for our sympathy because he knows that he’ll get it anyway, and not just because the purpose of Rockwell’s character is to ensure that we do. It’s Chris’ job to make rooting for the bad guys feel like the right choice. It’s the cornerstone of America’s post-war foreign policy. 

So while Chris might be cut from the same cloth as John Wayne (to the extent that Monument Valley is revealed to be a place of great importance to him), his arc is aimed in the opposite direction of the one that Ethan Edwards traces across “The Searchers”; Chris is a major asshole this movie gradually puckers into a wayward hero, and while it’s all too easy to root for him to complete that transformation before time runs out, at no point does “Wild Horse Nine” sell us on the premise that it would mean anything in the end — even to him. 

The movie, blessedly, isn’t Catholic enough to offer Chris a big moment of divine expiation; in lieu of building to a grand confession, he and Lee simply run afoul of their CIA higher-ups until their PTO turns into a matter of American national security. Guns are fired. Hostages are taken. The word “fuck” is used like a punctuation mark, and regrets are muttered into the wind long after there’s any way for them to matter. 

It all gets a bit too busy and madcap as “Wild Horse Nine” — freighted with sadness during even its cheekiest bits, as is McDonagh’s way — scrambles to make up for the general listlessness of its first half. Never as funny as it is sardonic, and always reaching so hard to be more of both, the film’s most successful moments are mined from the ambient tension between memory and erasure.

Chris, we begin to suspect, would do anything to forget what he’s done, and his own mind is graciously willing to get him halfway there. The rest of the CIA will do anything it takes to make sure that Chris doesn’t share whatever it is that he still remembers. Surrounding them on all sides are statues that predated America by several hundred years, and will likely continue to watch over Rapa Nui long after our empire has been wiped away like a tear in the rain. In “Wild Horse Nine,” American interventionism is less effective as the set-up for some jokes than it is as their punchline.

Grade: B-

“Wild Horse Nine” premiered at the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Searchlight Pictures will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.

entry.title: ‘North of North’ Season 2 Review: Netflix’s Defiantly Nice Arctic Sitcom Is for the Warmhearted F**k-Ups
entry.summary: 'North of North' Season 2 sees Anna Lambe's single mom double down on "leveling up" — at work, in love, and for her cherished Inuk community. [REVIEW]
entry.content:
There are dozens of scenes that capture “North of North’s” digestible, defiant kindness, but my favorite arrives near the start of the second season’s second episode. Siaja (Anna Lambe) wakes up, grabs a glass of water, and promptly spits it out. The local water supply is contaminated (“They must’ve cranked those chemicals again,” her mom says), so Siaja heads to the nearest store to load up on jugs of clean water. Outside, there’s an elderly woman perched on her snowmobile, smoking a cigarette, who loudly hassles Siaja for a little charity.

“Must be nice,” the woman shouts, getting Siaja’s attention. “[You] buying filtered water. It’s too expensive [for me]. [I] gotta drink government pool water. Back in the day, we had nice ice straight from the river. Pure, nice, and healthy.”

Related Stories
‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken
‘Black Doves’ Review: Season 2 Sticks to Its Guns in Keira Knightley’s Excellent, Existential Spy Thriller

On that last word, “healthy,” the woman takes a drag from her cigarette, and while she’s doubled over coughing, Siaja takes her forceful hint and puts one of her water jugs in the woman’s cart. “Here, you take this,” Siaja says. The woman, speaking in Inuktitut, does not say “thank you”; she asks if she can keep the jug. Then she hacks a loogie into the snow as Siaja drives off, punctuating just how little the gesture means to her.

Now, it’s clear this woman knows exactly what she’s doing. She didn’t end up outside the town’s only source for clean water by accident, and Siaja knows it. But she also knows the woman is telling the truth: She’s too old to get ice for herself, and she’s too poor to afford purified water. Siaja also knows this woman is her elder, and elders should be taken care of. So after acquiescing in the moment, Siaja expands on the idea soon after: She grabs Alistair (Jay Ryan), her big, burly dad, and they go get blocks of ice from the river to deliver around town — for free.

Of course, it doesn’t go exactly as planned (the rivers aren’t all “pure” and “healthy” anymore), but Siaja’s chance encounter with the woman serves as the impetus for the entire episode: Siaja uses it to prove to her boss that she can be more than an assistant at the community center. She bonds with her dad, who she’s still getting to know. She sets a good example for her daughter, Bun (Keira Belle Cooper), and she still finds time to flirt with her crush, Kuuk (Braeden Clarke), in between deliveries.

Siaja is doing exactly what she set out to do from the start of the season: “level up” her life.

Reading it back now, the story sounds corny. But despite all that positive energy driving so many warm-hearted gestures, “North by North” never becomes saccharine. Siaja’s triumphs don’t feel like cheap schmaltz. They hit that tricky TV sweet spot, where characters’ helpful actions and benevolent intentions feel genuine even when, on paper, they seem too nice to be tolerable.

It helps, of course, that Siaja fucks up early and often. Nothing makes a win land like taking many embarrassing losses to get there, as she did in Season 1 after summoning the courage to leave her husband, get a job, and start fresh — with an adorable daughter in tow. In Season 2, her plan to charm tourists doesn’t go over as whimsically as she imagined. Her plan to get her own place doesn’t include dropping in the rankings on an endless waiting list for affordable housing. Her plan to ditch her small-minded ex-husband (who doesn’t appear in Season 2) doesn’t include sitting for rounds of speed-dating or waiting out a relationship that may never end.

Siaja’s self-actualization isn’t as easy as ditching the zero to get with the hero, even when she’s her own hero from the jump — it takes time to learn the ins and outs of public service, to connect with people, and to make sense of your own emotions. “North of North” respects each process while savoring her struggle through them. (Lambe’s comic timing remains pitch-perfect, and her ability to navigate tonal swings is just as sharp.)

Investing in Siaja’s incremental progress does wonders to keep “North of North” from feeling like forgettable fluff — especially when the back-half of Season 2 gets heavy wrestling with familial, cultural, and communal responsibilities — but none of it work without the attention to detail surrounding Siaja, too. When the first season premiered in January 2025, “North by North” earned plenty of well-deserved praise for its authenticity. The fictional town of Ice Cove represents real communities in Nunavet, the northernmost part of Canada within the Arctic Circle, and the series employed a heavily Indigenous cast and crew to help bring it to life.

And what life there is: Season 2 is rich with cultural specifics, from a Greenlandic mask-dancing celebration to public safety concerns. (Beyond the bad water, don’t forget to place your beer orders early! A birthday without a brewski could be your last!) Every episode whisks you away to a very cold, very kind small town, which is oh-so-welcoming on chilly winter evenings when you just want to bask in the season’s cozy glow.

Respecting and highlighting Inuk customs is step one. Step two expands the idea by grounding “North by North” in perspectives beyond their beloved lead screwup. That way, her work ethic and generosity stay sweet and meaningful (when overexposure could easily turn them sour) and the show’s overall tone avoids becoming rote. Siaja’s mom, Neevee (Maika Harper), is the sardonic balance her daughter demands, and how they flesh out her backstory to explain her sharp disposition offers some of the season’s strongest scenes. Helen (Mary Lynn Rajskub), Siaja’s boss, is an oblivious white lady desperate to be cherished as a leader, and her pushy ambitions help clarify Siaja’s unselfish aid to others (while generating laughs).

And then there’s the townsfolk, who may not always be as colorful as the woman demanding free water, but who share her fair yet formidable spirit. If Siaja’s community service was met with cheers and applause, it would be unbelievable. That’s not how citizens treat their local officials. But their measured disposition isn’t just authentic, it’s essential. Similarly, if the citizens were the butt of every joke (like in “Parks and Recreation”), Siaja’s dedication could feel misplaced. If they were mean, like too many real-life city council visitors, her above-and-beyond gestures could seem foolish. Instead, Siaja’s community is just there, living their own lives, waiting for her to get her shit together and do what’s right by them.

Nice shows are harder to pull off than they seem. Too nice and it’s all gloss, no substance. Not nice enough and a comfort watch quickly turns uncomfortable. “North of North” Season 2 not only finds the sweet spot, but expands on it to push its deft star to new heights and welcome in an even broader swath of Netflix’s sizable subscriber base. This one’s for sitcom fans and comfort TV enthusiasts, but also small town stalwarts, the winter-loving cold weather freaks (it’s me), elders who expect more from the younger generations, anyone who likes spending time in fresh perspectives, and especially the goodhearted fuck-ups who won’t stop trying until they get it right.

Grade: B

“North of North” Season 2 premieres Thursday, November 5 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.

entry.title: ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken
entry.summary: Executive produced by Ari Aster, György Pálfi's 'Hen' evokes 'EO' and 'Flow' in its animal POV on humanity's moral failures. Review.
entry.content:
Among the bleakest films ever made, Werner Herzog’s “Stroszek” (1977) famously ends not with the suicide of its title character, but with a haunting coda in which a chicken pecks at a miniature piano inside a surreal roadside tourist trap’s coin-operated display. It’s a visual metaphor for the inescapable banality of life on Earth, and for the dehumanizing work people are forced to do to disguise the many failures of the American Dream. It’s also the last thing that Joy Division frontman Ian Curtis saw before he killed himself. “Look into the eyes of a chicken,” Herzog has said, “and you will see real stupidity. It is a kind of bottomless stupidity, a fiending stupidity. They are the most horrifying, cannibalistic, and nightmarish creatures in the world.”

Related Stories
Robert Pattinson to Receive 2026 American Cinematheque Award
AI Movie ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Gets Serious with AI-Generated Grimes Cameo, Times Square Marketing Push, Oscar Screenings

That sentiment has long endured as modern cinema’s definitive stance on chickens (despite Aardman’s best efforts), but now, after witnessing the 50 years of entropy that followed “Stroszek,” Hungarian filmmaker György Pálfi is crying fowl. Chickens are not the most horrifying, cannibalistic, and nightmarish creatures in the world, he contends. We are. How can you tell? Easy: Just look at us through the eyes of a chicken.

A cute, cockeyed yarn that unspools like a feathered cross between “EO” and “Flow,” Pálfi’s “Hen” tells the story of a jet-black Leghorn chicken who escapes a Greek factory farm after she’s plucked from the rest of her flock because of the color of her plumage. A worker decides to take the bird home so that his wife can serve it for dinner, but our sly heroine — played by a brave hen named Feri, in addition to her seven indistinguishable stunt doubles — makes a daring escape when her captor stops his truck to refuel. But she’s snapped up again by the teeth of a dog named Titan, who carries the chicken back to the ramshackle seaside restaurant where his owner (Yannis Kokiasmenos) has much bigger problems than what to serve for dinner.

If the precise contours of those problems are a bit difficult to deduce, that’s probably because — as we’ve already established — this movie is told through the eyes of a chicken. Sometimes literally, thanks to Pálfi’s judicious deployment of POV, which is useful for times when our ruffled protagonist is, say, trapped inside a cardboard box (there’s an excellent bit where the hen starts moving the cardboard box from the inside, a “Metal Gear Solid”-inspired visual gag that proves typical of the director’s wry humor). And what does a chicken know of Europe’s ongoing migrant crisis? Of a protest between angry citizens and riot police? Of human trafficking, and the complications thereof? To judge by the film’s regular assortment of amusingly blank reaction shots, I’d wager “very little.” The titular hen doesn’t even think to look both ways when she crosses the road after flying the coop, let alone have a good answer as to why she’s doing it.

For the most part, the hen is focused on clucking her neck, surviving the pecking order at the restaurant farm where she winds up, and potentially even laying a few eggs of her own someday (we see her hatch in the movie’s first scene, but they grow up so fast). Most of the human drama is relegated to the distant background, as Pálfi mines the humor from his movie’s conceit by using the restaurant as a lens onto the hen’s predicament rather than the other way around. The people are mere archetypes, but some of the animals we meet appear so layered and inscrutable that you’d happily watch a three-hour Nathan Fielder documentary about them. (The terse and fiery courtship between the star hen and her most aggressive suitor is soundtracked by a classic Greek love song, a flourish that stands out in a film where desperate migrants are being left for dead just off-camera.)

Then again, couldn’t every film about — and starring — real live animals be considered a documentary to some extent? Feri the chicken has been trained by the best of the business, but she remains blissfully unaware of the camera, and Pálfi takes pains not to anthropomorphize her any more than necessary. Plenty of heightened enjoyment comes elsewhere, much of it laundered through Giorgos Karvelas’ saturated cinematography, Szabolcs Szoke’s hyper-dynamic score, and the furtive way Pálfi bends the film’s crafts into something that almost resembles a chicken’s idea of a Western.

Here, the hen is a hen is a hen, and while “Hen” is prone to long and repetitive stretches in which she basically just hens around as a result of that approach, the animal’s natural obliviousness is too crucial a contrast to our own willful antipathy for Pálfi to risk muddying the difference between the two. At the risk of making the movie’s side-eyed social commentary sound more didactic than it is in practice (save for one very pointed moment towards the end that explicitly affirms Herzog’s claim), “Hen” uses a chicken’s lack of moral responsibility to highlight the mandate we have to heed our own, no matter how effectively we’ve evolved to ignore it.

No matter how good we get at farming other species, and killing our own. Pálfi does very little to goose or otherwise manipulate our emotional attachment to his chicken star, but there’s still something to be said for how easily we become more invested in this witless hen’s fate than in that of the doomed people with whom she crosses paths. By the time it reaches its end, this strange but sober film starts to point back to the beginning, cutting from a single egg being squeezed out of a hen’s vent (Google says “vent”) to a vast sea of them bobbling around inside the factory’s machines. One is easy to follow, and to care about. Thousands are a statistic. We’re smart enough to farm other animals, but people — like chickens — won’t hesitate to eat each other the minute they get hungry.

Grade: B

Dekanalog will release “Hen” in theaters on Friday, November 6.

entry.title: Robert Pattinson to Receive 2026 American Cinematheque Award
entry.summary: Robert Pattinson, star of several 2026 films, including 'The Odyssey' and 'Primetime, will be the 40th recipient of the American Cinematheque Award.
entry.content:
The American Cinematheque Awards Gala is officially back on with actor Robert Pattinson, star of several films from 2026, from “Primetime” and “The Drama,” to “The Odyssey” and “Dune: Part Three,” as the 40th recipient. The milestone celebration will now take place on Tuesday, February 9, 2027, at The Beverly Hilton in Beverly Hills.

Previously, the 2026 edition of the fundraiser had been set for November 2, with “Project Hail Mary” star Ryan Gosling accepting the award, but the incoming Marvel Cinematic Universe actor had to drop out of the event a month before due to a scheduling conflict.

Now, prolific actor Pattinson will be the one to join a roster of honorees that include filmmakers and performers like Eddie Murphy, Steven Spielberg, Martin Scorsese, Jodie Foster, Denzel Washington, Nicole Kidman, George Clooney, and most importantly Michael B. Jordan, the most recent American Cinematheque Award recipient, who would go on to win the Oscar for Best Actor shortly afterwards for his performance in “Sinners.”

Related Stories
AI Movie ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Gets Serious with AI-Generated Grimes Cameo, Times Square Marketing Push, Oscar Screenings
Cannes 2026 Movies Sold: Kino Lorber Buys Clio Barnard’s BIFA Contender ‘I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning’

According to the organization, the prestigious American Cinematheque Award “recognizes extraordinary artists whose talent, vision, and contributions have made a lasting impact on cinema. Their passion and filmography not only exemplify excellence in filmmaking but also reflect the cinematic artistry and breadth of American Cinematheque’s programming, which bridges film history to its future and celebrates the theatrical experience.”

This upcoming milestone 40th presentation will mark an especially meaningful moment in the American Cinematheque’s history, celebrating both the remarkable legacy of the award and the organization’s enduring contributions to cinema.

Explaining why Pattinson would be receiving the award, American Cinematheque Board Chair Rick Nicita said in an official statement, “Rob has built an extraordinary career defined by his unwavering dedication to his craft, fearless creative choices, and remarkable versatility as an actor. From his collaborations with some of cinema’s most visionary filmmakers to his ability to captivate audiences in major studio blockbusters, Rob has continually challenged expectations and demonstrated the power of great storytelling.”

“Rob is the perfect choice to receive this award and join our esteemed list of artists who not only love cinema but continue to have a deep impact on our industry,” added Nicita. “We are thrilled that his filming schedule has allowed us the opportunity to recognize his exceptional contributions to film and we look forward to celebrating his continued achievements.”

The American Cinematheque Awards Gala serves as an annual fundraiser for the non-profit organization, supporting its year-round programming at the Aero Theatre in Santa Monica, Los Feliz 3 Theatre in Los Feliz, and Egyptian Theatre in Hollywood.

entry.title: AI Movie ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Gets Serious with AI-Generated Grimes Cameo, Times Square Marketing Push, Oscar Screenings
entry.summary: AI film 'Gods Don't Give Gifts' will feature a cameo from Grimes and will be advertised with a massive Times Square ad campaign.
entry.content:
When we first wrote about the coming release of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” the first fully AI-generated feature film being self-distributed into movie theaters in the U.S., it would’ve been easy to write the whole thing off as a stunt.

Coming from YouTuber Gossip Goblin, who has an impressive and loyal following, “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” started earning comps from the press (and from the producers themselves) to the success Markiplier found when he self-released his film “Iron Lung” and made $50 million worldwide in the process. Would that success translate for an AI movie? A recent example from China suggests that may not be the case.

Related Stories
Cannes 2026 Movies Sold: Kino Lorber Buys Clio Barnard’s BIFA Contender ‘I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning’
Sony Pictures Classics Buys Jean-Pierre Jeunet’s ‘Violette’

It’s clear though the team behind “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is treating this like a real project that needs to be seen in theaters and is worthy of serious critical consideration, and they’re doing that with real marketing dollars behind its theatrical push.

Today, Gossip Goblin announced that pop star Grimes is set to make a cameo in his film “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” as is YouTuber Mike Majlak, and their involvement is being revealed via a massive Times Square ad campaign that is also launching today, all ahead of the film’s release next month on December 4. Gossip Goblin is even launching a contest for people to use AI to create their own short films within the universe of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” that can net the winning creator $15,000.

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts” also sparked some headlines in the last few months with the news that the producers are plotting an Oscar campaign for Best Animated Feature. Turns out some FYC screenings have already started and a digital campaign begins at the end of November. All of the above suggests some real belief in the project, and with a collective 16 million views of the trailer thus far, they have reason to believe.

“We’ve been heartened already by the reaction,” producer Edward Saatchi of Fable Studios said in a statement. “One Oscar-Nominated animated film director compared ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ after seeing it to ‘2001,’ and we’ve had great feedback from Pixar folks (part of Fable’s team is ex-Pixar and we hugely respect their work).”

Zack London, the man behind the moniker Gossip Goblin, in speaking with IndieWire ahead of the announcement, said he’s “fully cognizant” of the controversy around putting a movie made with AI into theaters, and he acknowledges that all of this is “a big, unproven hypothesis.” But he says it would be “disingenuous to write it all off” as just an AI movie or not a real project.

Getting screens is easy, but the real battle is making people believe there are actually humans behind this movie, even if the images are all generated by AI. Roughly 30 to 35 people are credited in the making of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” and a behind-the-scenes documentary that is also in the works is aimed to humanize the process of making the movie. It includes interviews with the film’s composer and voice actors and shows its Foley guy doing real post-production work. Even the act of getting a real person like Grimes in the film — whose image is generated to resemble her but who does real voice acting — required an elaborate process of photo mashing atop existing character design to fit her into the movie, as well as contacting the model makers themselves to remove built-in censors for generating images of a public figure’s likeness.

On one hand, “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” can be viewed as a scrappy indie made by a team of creatives, not just a sole prompter working alone, making a movie that wouldn’t exist otherwise. On the other hand, many would argue that the visuals on display would normally require a team of thousands to bring to life along with millions of dollars. Depending on where you fall on that spectrum may determine whether you also buy a ticket to see it.

But London and Saatchi have grander ambitions with “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” and AI filmmaking beyond just what it can do at the box office. Saatchi says that for as many great CG animated films have been released in the last 30 years since “Toy Story” first hit theaters, they’ve arguably all looked similar and been made with the same techniques. He views “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” as the next “Toy Story” moment in animation, with a movie that aims to look psychedelic and otherworldly, something that looks unique and looks like it could only be the product of AI generative models. Other films may use AI to create something cheaply that looks like a Pixar movie, but London wanted to make something that looked like nothing else.

“Pixar set the look for animated films in the ’90s — they didn’t use technology to more cheaply make a film that looked like ‘Beauty and the Beast,’ they created a radically new aesthetic with ‘Toy Story,'” Saatchi said. “That’s what ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ represents: a wild new aesthetic for animated films that will define much of animated, actor-voiced films in the coming decades. This is that ‘Toy Story’ moment for our generation — a radical departure for animated films — you only need to see Grimes’ brilliant performance in the film to understand how much things are about to change for animated movies. And we hope the Academy will recognize that a film that is seminal (the first AI film), wildly technically novel and most importantly good deserves a nomination.”
